title: How Our Brains Influence Each Other
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of recognizing our interconnectedness with others and cultivating compassion in the face of social injustices. By acknowledging our own limitations and taking action to expand our connections, we can work towards creating a more just and equitable world. This involves letting go of materialistic views and embracing a sense of community and shared humanity, particularly through Buddhist practice and honoring the lives and deaths of those who have been targeted by racism and hatred.

So, in the fifth lesson, in *Seven and a Half Lessons About the Brain* by Dr.
Lisa Feldman Barrett, this chapter is all about how our brains influence each other.
The previous chapter we looked at was pretty far out: our brains basically create reality.
Our brains have the ability to create a predicted future reality that we experience as if it was really happening, which is all pretty mind-blowing, since we think that's not what's happening.

We think we're experiencing what's happening now in real time and looking out at the objective world through the portals of our senses, but she painted a much more complex picture, the brain assembling reality as a controlled hallucination.

And remember the overall theme of the book, her root understanding of how the brain works: it's all about our stability and survival, including our thinking, including our perceptions, including, of course, the regulation of the physiological systems of the body.

But this chapter, at first glance, doesn't seem quite as far out.
We already know that we influence each other, right?
That's pretty obvious.

Probably our blood pressure drops a little bit when we're hanging out with someone we enjoy.
So what's interesting about this chapter is that, yes, this is obvious, but it also goes much, much deeper than that.
This influence between us is deeply powerful in a systematic way, through all of our systems, and it can operate in both a positive direction and a negative direction.

And our propensity for this is not just a neat little extra thing, kind of cool, but maybe actually quite fundamental to the efficiency of the system, so that over the long haul we're more likely to survive and reproduce.

So it goes really deep, is what she's pointing out, how deeply we influence each other, to the point where it starts to become a little dubious to think about ourselves as separate people.
So this all sounds like Buddhism, right?
When we're together, we're not only operating an intense, incredibly complicated networked mind, networked brain, I mean, but between us we're also forming a certain kind of neurological network.
She presented a few bits of evidence around the positive side of this, a phenomenon called co-regulation.
One is that when you're with somebody you care about, your breathing often synchronizes, as well as the actual beating of your heart, the rhythm of your heart.
And this is apparently not just that we feel in sync and in harmony and that that also expresses physically, but more that our brains now don't have to work quite as hard.
There's a little advantage if they can share the load of regulating even apparently automatic processes like breathing and beating hearts.
We're literally cooperating in the rhythm of breathing and the beating of the heart, and that makes it easier for both of us.
So we use up a little less energy.
So that's good.

Another, and these are based on studies that she talks about in the footnotes, is that people in loving and positive intimate relationships tend to have stronger immune systems and are literally less likely to get sick.
And if you're already sick with cancer or heart disease, some other major illness, you're more likely to get better if you're in a positive, loving, close relationship.
I'm not sure exactly how the studies defined what that relationship is.
So somehow the two brains even help each other cope with the complex physiological processes of immune response.
It's crazy, really.
Not the way we think.
A third is that if a loved one is in pain, and I'd seen this one before, holding their hand reduces their pain.
Again, we tend to be aware of these things, but the way we think about them is shallow compared to the neuroscience she's presenting.

The one we're probably all aware of is how vigilant our system is for threat, anything that's threatening.

The title of the chapter is "Your Brain Secretly Works with Other Brains."
Secretly.

We welcome you to May We Gather, a national Buddhist memorial for Asian American ancestors.

Today, May 4th, 2021, marks the 49th day since eight people, six of them women of Asian descent, were killed in a mass shooting in Georgia.

Here in this temple and across the country online, we will make merit together today.

When our Chinese immigrant ancestors came to these shores in the 1850s, we faced exclusion and violence.
Our Buddhist and Taoist temples were desecrated and set ablaze.

Our Buddhist faith was deemed un-American.

When our South and Southeast Asian parents and grandparents arrived in this country in the 1970s, many fleeing wars inflamed by the American military, we were told our cultures and Buddhist traditions didn't belong.
In the face of nearly two centuries of xenophobia and systemic violence, Asian American Buddhists have long joined together to rebuild our communities.
Piece by broken piece, we sutured the jagged edges of altars, statues, incense burners, and our very bodies and minds back together.
This mending is part of our Buddhist practice in America.
Each act of rejoining reveals how compassion can arise out of racial suffering, how fragments are inseparable from wholeness.
We mend them as a declaration of our interconnectedness, as an expression of gratitude to our ancestors, and as a way to cultivate the karmic conditions for American Buddhism's continued flourishing.

As we confront yet another wave of violence, vandalism, and exclusion targeting Asian Americans and Asian American Buddhists, let us honor our ancestors by continuing their legacy of gathering and mending.

He is here through his teachings, which links the past to the present and each of us to one another.
